I am 75 years old. I have farmed these fields in Quzhou for more than 50 years. My husband passed away ten years ago, and my children have moved to the city, but I still manage my land myself with help from neighbors during harvest. I have about 6 mu of good flat land, and I know every inch of it.

This year, I will stick to what I know best: **winter wheat followed by summer maize** on all 6 mu. I am too old to chase after cotton — that crop needs spraying every few days, and my back cannot handle 13 trips with the sprayer. Wheat and maize are reliable. The machines come to the village for sowing and harvest, and the grain station buys them at a fair price. I also keep a small garden by my house for vegetables, but my real livelihood is the field crops.

For the **winter wheat** that is already in the ground, I sowed it last October using *Jimai 22*, an improved variety that does well here. I used the rotary tiller before sowing, as I have always done. Now that spring has arrived, I will irrigate it three times: once in early spring if the winter was dry, once at the jointing stage, and once during grain filling. I will apply about 40 jin of urea per mu as topdressing at jointing, plus the compound fertilizer I put down as base. I expect about 1,000 jin of wheat per mu if the weather cooperates. I will spray insecticide twice, herbicide once, and fungicide once to protect the crop.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I will immediately plant **summer maize** using *Denghai 605*, a hybrid seed that yields well. I will not till the soil — I will sow directly into the wheat stubble. No-tillage saves me fuel, labor, and time, and the young maize does fine. I will irrigate twice: once when it is young if June is hot and dry, and once at the big trumpet stage. Two sprays for insects and one for weeds will be enough. I hope for 1,100 jin per mu.

I know my land. I do not need fancy experiments. Wheat and maize feed me, and the leftover grain brings in cash for medicine and for my grandchildren when they visit.
